external-dependency, datastore, or entrypoint), each with a stable ID and a

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.
I'll start by exploring the codebase to build the system map.

payload_or_id.description: kvstore/api.py: the only client-facing operation, get_value(cache, key). Calls Cache.get, catches StorageError to increment kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome="error"} and re-raises, otherwise increments outcome="success" and returns the value. This is the sole point where client-visible read behaviour is instrumented; it cannot distinguish a correct cached value from a stale one, since both are plain returns from Cache.get.

kvstore/cache.py: in-process, in-memory dict of key -> Entry(value, inserted_at_ms) sitting in front of Storage. Cache.get returns a cached entry if present and never re-consults storage for an already-cached key; on a miss it reads through to Storage and inserts an entry stamped with time.time()*1000 (milliseconds). It expires nothing on its own -- removal happens only via Cache.evict, called by the evictor. Cache.evict is also available to writers but no writer in this package calls it. Entirely uninstrumented: no size, hit/miss, or age metrics.

kvstore/storage.py: backing flat-file key-value store at a configured Path, one "key,value" pair per line. get() scans the whole file linearly and returns the first matching key (or None when the file is absent or the key is missing); put() reads the entire file into a dict, sets the key, mkdirs the parent, and rewrites the whole file in a single non-atomic write_text. Both wrap OSError in StorageError. Keys and values containing the ',' delimiter or a newline are not escaped. Uninstrumented: no latency, size, or error metrics of its own -- errors are only visible where a caller happens to count them.

The local filesystem path holding the flat-file store (Storage._path) and its parent directory. Supplies durability, capacity, and permissions for every read and write; whole-file read and whole-file rewrite on each put mean its size drives read and write cost directly. Failures surface to the service only as OSError -> StorageError.

kvstore/evictor.py: run_eviction_pass(cache) walks Cache.items() and evicts every entry where now - entry.inserted_at_ms > TTL_SECONDS (300.0), returning the number removed so a caller can observe progress. It is the only mechanism that bounds cache size or bounds staleness of a cached entry. Its `now` is time.time() in seconds while Entry.inserted_at_ms is in milliseconds, so the comparison operand is a large negative number and the expiry condition is never true. The return value is the only signal it produces and nothing in this repo records it.

The periodic caller that is meant to invoke evictor.run_eviction_pass on a schedule. Referenced by evictor.py's docstring ("a caller (e.g. a scheduler loop)") but NOT present in this repository -- no module calls run_eviction_pass. Recorded as a component because the eviction path only bounds the cache if something drives it, so "the pass never runs" is a distinct failure from "the pass runs and evicts nothing", and the two need separate detection.

kvstore/admin.py: internal, non-client-facing write path, update_value(storage, cache, key, value). Not reachable from external clients. It calls Storage.put only; it accepts a Cache argument but never calls cache.evict(key), so a key already resident in the cache keeps serving its pre-write value indefinitely. Uninstrumented: no write counter, no error counter, no invalidation signal.

The periodic data-sync job that drives admin.update_value, named in kvstore/__init__.py and admin.py as the intended caller of the internal write path. Its scheduling and implementation live outside this repository, so its run cadence, success/failure, and per-run write volume are wholly unobserved from here; it is the only known source of writes and therefore the only thing that makes cached values stale.

No HTTP exposition server (start_http_server) or pushgateway call exists anywhere in this repository, so nothing in-tree makes these counters reachable by a scraper -- the exposition/scrape path is an unverified assumption and every alert recommendation in this run depends on it.

event.text:
Phase 1 accepted — 9 components in the system map.

**The service** (`kvstore`, ~150 lines of Python, one dependency: `prometheus_client==0.26.0`):

```
sm-data-sync-job ──> sm-admin-write-path ──┬──> sm-storage ──> sm-backing-file
                                           └──> sm-cache ────────┘ (read-through)
sm-get-value-api ──> sm-cache
              └────> sm-prometheus-client-registry
sm-evictor-scheduler ──> sm-evictor ──> sm-cache
```

**Entry points (2).** `sm-get-value-api` is the only client-facing one — `get_value(cache, key)`, the sole instrumented point in the codebase. `sm-admin-write-path` is internal-only, driven by an out-of-repo sync job.

**Three things I recorded deliberately, because they set up the failure chains:**

1. **`sm-evictor-scheduler` is in the map but not in the repo.** Nothing calls `run_eviction_pass`. I listed it anyway because "the pass never runs" and "the pass runs and evicts nothing" are different failures needing different detection — and the second one is real: the evictor compares `time.time()` (seconds) against `inserted_at_ms` (milliseconds), so the expiry condition is never true. The cache has no bound at all.

2. **`sm-prometheus-client-registry` is an external dependency, not just a library.** There is no `start_http_server` and no pushgateway call anywhere in the tree. The one existing metric may not be reachable by any scraper — and every alert I recommend in phase 4 will depend on that exposition path existing. Flagging it now rather than building four phases on an unverified assumption.

3. **`sm-admin-write-path` takes a `Cache` argument it never uses.** It writes to storage and never calls `cache.evict(key)`. Combined with `Cache.get` never re-consulting storage for a cached key, and the evictor never expiring anything: a written key that is already cached serves its old value permanently, and the request counter returns `outcome="success"` for every one of those reads.

The observability baseline is one counter, `kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome}`, at the outermost layer. The cache, storage, evictor, and write path emit nothing — the evictor's eviction count is returned to a caller that doesn't exist.

Ready for phase 2 (failure modes) when you are.
what about the admin write path in admin.py -- it's not reachable from api.py's public surface at all, does that matter here?

It matters, but it cuts the opposite way from exclusion — it's the reason the write path needs *more* attention here, not less.

**Reachability from `api.py` isn't the relevant kind of reachability.** `admin.update_value` and `get_value` share no call edge, but they share two pieces of mutable state: the backing file and the cache dict. That's the coupling. A call-graph-based scope ("what can the public surface reach?") would drop `admin.py` and would thereby drop the *cause* of the worst failure in this system, keeping only its last link — a read returning a wrong value with `outcome="success"`. That is exactly the "failure chains, not just user-visible ends" problem: the user-visible end is in `api.py`, but every upstream link is in `admin.py` and `evictor.py`.

**"Not reachable from external clients" is a statement about exposure, not about impact.** It means an attacker can't call it and a user can't trigger it. It doesn't mean it can't corrupt what users see — and here it does, on every write to an already-cached key.

**Being internal makes it harder to detect, not easier.** A client-facing bug generates client-facing signal: errors, retries, complaints, a moving `outcome="error"` counter. A stale read generates none of those. Nobody gets an error, the counter increments `success`, and the sync job that caused it lives outside this repo and reports nothing in-tree. The absence of a client path removes the detection channel while leaving the fault intact.

Where it *does* legitimately change the analysis is priority and alert shape in later phases: no external caller means no request-rate or latency SLO on this path, no user-facing error budget, and no traffic-driven alert. Detection has to come from the write side (did the sync job run, did it write, was the cache invalidated) or from staleness measurement on the read side — not from anything resembling an endpoint alert. I'll carry that into phases 3 and 4.

I tightened the map entry so a later phase can't drop it on reachability grounds:

Accepted. The entry now records both the scope justification and the constraint on what alert shapes are valid for it, so phase 4 doesn't reach for endpoint-style alerting on a path with no callers.

One thing I should flag as genuinely uncertain rather than settled: I've assumed the sync job actually writes on some cadence, because `__init__.py` and `admin.py` both describe it as periodic. If it turns out to be manual or rare, the stale-read failure mode stays real but its likelihood drops a lot, and the write-side liveness alert I'm planning would be noise. That's outside this repo, so I can't resolve it from the code — if you know the answer, it'll sharpen phase 4.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;

Working through the chains — each user-visible symptom traced back to the code-level link that produces it.

payload_or_id.name: get_value returns a value that has since been overwritten
payload_or_id.description: A client calls get_value(key) and receives a value that no longer matches the current truth. Two distinct divergences produce the same symptom: cache-vs-storage (the sync job wrote a new value to the file but the cached Entry still holds the old one) and storage-vs-source (the sync job never wrote at all). Silent in every respect: no exception, no log, and kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome="success"} increments exactly as it does for a correct read, so the existing metric cannot distinguish this from healthy traffic. Critical because with no working expiry the divergence is permanent, not transient -- the affected key serves the wrong value for the life of the process.

payload_or_id.name: get_value returns None for a key that exists in storage
payload_or_id.description: A client reads a key and gets None although the key is present in the backing file. Main path: Cache.get caches the miss itself (Entry(value=None)), so any key read before it was first written keeps returning None permanently once the sync job creates it -- negative cache poisoning that no expiry clears. Also reached when the backing file has lost records. Indistinguishable at the API from a legitimately absent key: get_value returns None and counts outcome="success".

payload_or_id.name: get_value returns another key's value (delimiter collision)
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get uses line.partition(",") and matches on the segment before the first comma. A stored key containing a comma collides with a shorter key: writing key "a,b" value "v" produces the line "a,b,v", and a read of key "a" matches it and returns "b,v". The client receives a well-formed value belonging to a different key, with no error and outcome="success". Critical because it is a silent correctness violation that can cross tenant or entity boundaries depending on the key scheme.

payload_or_id.name: get_value raises StorageError to the caller
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get misses, Storage.get hits an OSError, and the resulting StorageError propagates through api.get_value to the client after incrementing kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome="error"}. This is the one failure in the system with existing instrumentation and a real signal. Note the cache masks its own blast radius: already-cached keys keep being served from memory, so the error rate reflects only miss traffic and understates how broken storage is.

payload_or_id.name: Process exhausts memory and dies; all reads fail
payload_or_id.description: The cache dict grows until the process hits its memory limit and is OOM-killed or begins thrashing. Every in-flight and subsequent read fails until it restarts. Total loss of the client-facing operation. The counter stops moving rather than recording errors, so detection must come from absence of traffic and from process/memory signals, not from outcome="error".

payload_or_id.name: get_value latency grows with backing-file size
payload_or_id.description: Client-visible slowdown on reads. Every cache miss costs a full read_text plus a linear scan of the whole file, so miss latency grows linearly with the number of stored keys; a cold cache after restart converts a burst of traffic into a burst of whole-file reads. Unmeasurable today: there is no latency metric anywhere in the codebase, only a request counter, so this degrades until a client complains.

payload_or_id.name: Backing file truncated or partially written; many keys lost at once
payload_or_id.description: Storage.put rewrites the entire dataset with a single write_text. A crash, OOM kill, or ENOSPC partway through leaves the file truncated or half-written, destroying records for keys unrelated to the write in progress. Clients then read None (or a garbled final line) for keys that previously existed. The loss is silent on the read path and, for keys still cached, invisible until the process restarts.

payload_or_id.name: Write path never invalidates the cached entry
payload_or_id.description: admin.update_value(storage, cache, key, value) calls storage.put and never calls cache.evict(key), despite receiving the Cache specifically as an argument and Cache.evict existing for this purpose. Every write to a key that is currently cached creates an immediate cache-vs-storage divergence. This is the root link of the stale-read chain and is present unconditionally in the current code -- it is not a rare runtime event.

payload_or_id.name: Cache.get never re-consults storage for a cached key
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get returns self._entries[key].value whenever the key is present and only reads through to Storage on a miss. There is no revalidation, no max-age check at read time, and no write-through. Consequently the eviction pass is the sole mechanism that can ever correct a diverged entry, which makes the whole staleness story depend on the evictor working -- and it does not. Documented separately from the evictor bug because a revalidating read path would contain the damage even with the evictor broken.

payload_or_id.name: Eviction pass evicts nothing: seconds compared against milliseconds
payload_or_id.description: evictor.run_eviction_pass computes now = time.time() (seconds) and tests now - entry.inserted_at_ms > TTL_SECONDS, while Cache stores inserted_at_ms = time.time() * 1000. The left side is roughly -1.7e12 and never exceeds 300.0, so expired_keys is always empty and the function always returns 0. The pass runs, does no work, and reports success. Two overlapping puts mean the later writer's snapshot omits the earlier writer's key, which is erased from the store. No locking, no compare-and-swap, no error. Warning rather than critical only because the single known writer may be serial -- if the sync job is ever parallelised or a second writer is added, this becomes routine silent data loss.

payload_or_id.title: Keys or values containing ',' or newline corrupt the file format
payload_or_id.description: The flat-file format is "key,value" per line with no escaping or quoting on either write or read. A comma in a key shifts the key/value boundary (producing fm-wrong-value-returned-key-collision); a newline in a value injects an additional record that will be parsed as a real key on the next read; a value containing a comma survives a round trip by luck of partition() but is re-serialised identically and remains ambiguous. Corruption is introduced at write time and only observed much later at read time, which makes attribution hard.

payload_or_id.title: Every miss reads and scans the entire backing file
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get calls read_text() on the whole file and scans lines until it matches, and Storage.put reads and rewrites all of it. Both are O(dataset size) with the whole file resident in memory per call. Cost grows silently with the store and is bounded only by the cache hit ratio; there is no size, latency, or IO instrumentation to show it rising.

payload_or_id.title: Restart empties the cache and converts traffic into whole-file reads
payload_or_id.description: The cache is process-local with no warmup and no persistence, so every restart or deploy drops it to empty. Each subsequent request is a miss doing a full-file read; concurrent misses for the same key are not coalesced, so N simultaneous requests do N independent whole-file reads. Produces a latency spike after every restart, and its magnitude grows as the dataset grows.

payload_or_id.title: get_value returns None for a key that exists in storage
payload_or_id.description: A client reads a key and gets None although the key is present in the backing file. Main path: Cache.get caches the miss itself (Entry(value=None)), so any key read before it was first written keeps returning None permanently once the sync job creates it -- negative cache poisoning that no expiry clears. Also reached when the backing file has lost records. Indistinguishable at the API from a legitimately absent key: get_value returns None and counts outcome="success".

payload_or_id.title: get_value returns another key's value (delimiter collision)
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get uses line.partition(",") and matches on the segment before the first comma. A stored key containing a comma collides with a shorter key: writing key "a,b" value "v" produces the line "a,b,v", and a read of key "a" matches it and returns "b,v". The client receives a well-formed value belonging to a different key, with no error and outcome="success". Critical because it is a silent correctness violation that can cross tenant or entity boundaries depending on the key scheme.

payload_or_id.title: get_value raises StorageError to the caller
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get misses, Storage.get hits an OSError, and the resulting StorageError propagates through api.get_value to the client after incrementing kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome="error"}. This is the one failure in the system with existing instrumentation and a real signal -- alertable today with a new rule and no new metric. Note the cache masks its own blast radius: already-cached keys keep being served from memory, so the error rate reflects only miss traffic and understates how broken storage is.

payload_or_id.title: Process exhausts memory and dies; all reads fail
payload_or_id.description: The cache dict grows until the process hits its memory limit and is OOM-killed or begins thrashing. Every in-flight and subsequent read fails until it restarts. Total loss of the client-facing operation. The counter stops moving rather than recording errors, so detection must come from absence of traffic and from process/memory signals, not from outcome="error".

payload_or_id.title: get_value latency grows with backing-file size
payload_or_id.description: Client-visible slowdown on reads. Every cache miss costs a full read_text plus a linear scan of the whole file, so miss latency grows linearly with the number of stored keys; a cold cache after restart converts a burst of traffic into a burst of whole-file reads. Unmeasurable today: there is no latency metric anywhere in the codebase, only a request counter, so this degrades until a client complains.

payload_or_id.title: Backing file truncated or partially written; many keys lost at once

A crash, OOM kill, or ENOSPC partway through leaves the file truncated or half-written, destroying records for keys unrelated to the write in progress. Clients then read None (or a garbled final line) for keys that previously existed. The loss is silent on the read path and, for keys still cached, invisible until the process restarts.

payload_or_id.title: Write path never invalidates the cached entry
payload_or_id.description: admin.update_value(storage, cache, key, value) calls storage.put and never calls cache.evict(key), despite receiving the Cache specifically as an argument and Cache.evict existing for this purpose. Every write to a key that is currently cached creates an immediate cache-vs-storage divergence. This is the root link of the stale-read chain and is present unconditionally in the current code -- it is not a rare runtime event.

payload_or_id.title: Cache.get never re-consults storage for a cached key
payload_or_id.exclusion_reason: Unconditional design property rather than a runtime event: it is true at every instant the current code is deployed, so any detector for it would fire continuously from the moment it is installed and would carry no information about the system's present state. payload_or_id.description: Cache.get returns self._entries[key].value whenever the key is present and only reads through to Storage on a miss: no revalidation, no read-time max-age check, no write-through. payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass evicts nothing: seconds compared against milliseconds
payload_or_id.description: evictor.run_eviction_pass computes now = time.time() (seconds) and tests now - entry.inserted_at_ms > TTL_SECONDS, while Cache stores inserted_at_ms = time.time() * 1000. payload_or_id.title: Nothing invokes run_eviction_pass
payload_or_id.description: No module in this repository calls evictor.run_eviction_pass; the scheduler is described in a docstring only (sm-evictor-scheduler). Both must be detectable independently -- pass ran, and pass did work.

payload_or_id.title: Cache grows without bound
payload_or_id.description: Nothing ever removes an entry from Cache._entries, so resident set size tracks the number of distinct keys ever requested for the life of the process. Warning rather than critical because it degrades over hours or days and there is a window to act, but only if something is watching cache size, and nothing is.

Both persist because nothing expires entries.

event.text:
Phase 2 accepted — 25 failure modes: 7 user-visible, 18 upstream links. 15 critical, 10 warning. Coverage split: **1 alertable today, 23 metric-gap, 1 excluded.**

**The chains.** Four converge on the same three root links:

```
fm-ttl-comparison-unit-mismatch ─┐
fm-eviction-pass-never-scheduled ┼─> fm-cache-unbounded-growth ──> fm-service-unavailable-oom
fm-negative-caching-of-misses ───┘

fm-write-does-not-invalidate-cache ─┐
fm-ttl-comparison-unit-mismatch ────┼─> fm-outdated-value-served  (silent, permanent)
fm-sync-job-stalled ────────────────┤
fm-storage-write-error ─────────────┘

fm-unescaped-delimiter-corruption ──> fm-wrong-value-returned-key-collision
fm-nonatomic-whole-file-rewrite ──┬─> fm-mass-data-loss
fm-disk-full ─────────────────────┘
```

The evictor's unit bug is the highest-leverage node — it's the shared upstream of both the OOM chain and the staleness chain.

**Three findings worth your attention:**

**Only one failure mode is detectable today.** `fm-read-errors-returned-to-clients` — and even that understates itself, because the cache serves already-cached keys from memory during a storage outage, so the error rate tracks miss traffic rather than how broken storage is.

**The existing metric actively lies during the worst failures.** I filed that as its own failure mode (`fm-silent-success-accounting`) rather than leaving it as a phase-3 coverage note. Stale values, poisoned `None`s, and collision-induced wrong values all take the non-raising branch and count `outcome="success"`. The service reports 100% healthy precisely while serving wrong data — that causes operator error, not just missing information.

**I split the evictor into two failure modes deliberately.** `fm-ttl-comparison-unit-mismatch` and `fm-eviction-pass-never-scheduled` need independent detectors: a liveness signal ("the pass ran") won't catch the arithmetic bug, because a broken pass completes normally and returns 0. And fixing the arithmetic changes nothing if no caller drives it. Phase 3 will need both a run counter and an evictions-performed counter.

**One exclusion.** `fm-cache-never-rechecks-storage` — an unconditional design property, true at every instant the current code is deployed. Any detector fires continuously from install and carries no information about present state. Its runtime consequences are covered where they're observable, so excluding it loses no detection; it stays documented because it's why staleness here is permanent rather than bounded.

**Two severity calls that rest on unverified assumptions**, both flagged in the entries: `fm-sync-job-stalled` is warning on the assumption the job is genuinely periodic (docstring only), and `fm-concurrent-put-lost-update` is warning only because the single known writer may be serial. If a second writer is ever added, that becomes routine silent data loss and should be critical.

Ready for phase 3.

Phase 3 -- metric coverage: inventory the metrics this codebase actually implements as
Metric entries (tied to where each is emitted in the code), then set every failure
mode's coverage status: `alertable` (implemented metrics suffice; only an alert rule is
missing), `metric-gap` (implemented metrics cannot detect it adequately; propose the
metric change needed), or `excluded` (record the reason). Every metric recommendation
must name the failure mode(s) it serves and state whether it is a new metric or a
change to an existing one. Propose every entry through `propose_edits`, tagged for
phase 3.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.

- Python: the `prometheus_client` library (Counter, Gauge, Histogram, Summary
  definitions and their `.labels(...)` call sites).
- Go: `prometheus/client_golang` (`prometheus.NewCounter`/`NewGauge`/`NewHistogram`

payload_or_id.proposed_site: kvstore/api.py:26-33, with Cache.get returning (value, source) or exposing a hit/miss signal so api.py can label without reaching into cache internals.
payload_or_id.description: CHANGE to the one existing metric, not a replacement -- keep the name and the outcome label so existing history and any current alert rule survive. Add source=cache_hit|storage_read and result=found|not_found. This makes three things measurable that are invisible today: the cache hit ratio (which governs how badly a storage outage is masked, and whose collapse after a restart is the cold-cache stampede), the not_found rate (a step change means negative-cache poisoning or record loss rather than client behaviour), and the split between answers served from memory and answers verified against storage. Cardinality stays bounded at 2x2x2 -- do NOT add a key label, which is unbounded and is the one label that would look most useful here.

payload_or_id.proposed_site: kvstore/api.py, around the cache.get call in get_value.
payload_or_id.description: There is no timing instrumentation of any kind in this codebase, so no latency failure is currently measurable at any layer. Labeling by source separates the cheap hit path from the expensive miss path, so a rising p99 can be attributed to hit-ratio collapse versus storage getting slower rather than just observed.

payload_or_id.proposed_site: kvstore/storage.py, in both get() and put(), incremented on the success return and in the except OSError handler before raising StorageError.

payload_or_id.proposed_site: kvstore/storage.py, set from len(existing) at the end of a successful put(); optionally refreshed by a periodic stat/parse so it does not go stale between writes.
payload_or_id.description: Detects the whole class of silent data loss: a truncated write, an ENOSPC mid-rewrite, and a lost-update race all show as the record count dropping or failing to grow, none of which raises an exception and none of which is visible on the read path until someone asks for a missing key. payload_or_id.proposed_site: kvstore/cache.py -- set to len(self._entries) after insertion in get() and after removal in evict(); or refreshed once per eviction pass, which already walks every entry.
payload_or_id.description: The cache has no bound, no size limit, and no size signal. This gauge is the early link in the OOM chain: it rises monotonically hours or days before process_resident_memory_bytes approaches the limit, which converts a hard critical failure (fm-service-unavailable-oom) into a warning with a window to act. process_resident_memory_bytes comes free from the default collectors once exposition exists, but it moves late and does not attribute the growth to the cache -- this does.

It is also the closest proxy for the staleness bound the system is supposed to guarantee: an entry's age is the maximum time it can have been diverging from storage. Implementation note: this metric is itself vulnerable to the exact bug it detects, so derive it from the same timestamp field the evictor compares and unit-test it against an entry older than the TTL.

Both metrics are needed; error counting alone leaves the worst case uncovered.

Node-level filesystem capacity monitoring is the natural earlier detector but sits outside this codebase.

Honest limitation: if no interruption ever occurs, this failure mode is undetectable and harmless, so the metrics here detect its consequence, not its presence. Silent by construction -- both writers succeed and neither errors. Detectable only as a reconciliation: successful writes of new keys accumulating faster than the storage record count grows. Phase 3 accepted. Inventory: **1 metric**, `kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome}` at `api.py:19`. No exposition endpoint, no logging, no timing instrumentation anywhere — confirmed by grep across the tree.

**Coverage: 2 alertable, 22 metric-gap, 1 excluded.** 14 recommendations — 13 new, 1 change to the existing counter.

**One status revised from phase 2.** I had `fm-service-unavailable-oom` as metric-gap; it's **alertable**. Once the registry is exposed, `up`, `absent()` on the existing counter, and prometheus_client's free default collectors (`process_resident_memory_bytes`, `process_start_time_seconds`) detect process death with rules alone. But that only tells you the service is *already down* — the preventable link, `fm-cache-unbounded-growth`, stays a metric-gap needing `kvstore_cache_entries`. Alerting only on the crash is choosing to find out too late.

**The blocking item.** `mr-metrics-exposition` isn't really a metric — it's the prerequisite. No `start_http_server`, no WSGI app, no pushgateway. Counters increment into a process-local registry and are discarded at exit. Everything else here and every phase-4 alert is inert until it exists.

**Deliberate choices worth reviewing:**

- **One `change`, not a replacement.** Adding `source` and `result` to the existing counter keeps the name and `outcome` label so any current history and rules survive. Bounded at 2×2×2 — I explicitly ruled out a `key` label, which is unbounded and the one that looks most useful here.
- **Two evictor detectors, not one.** `runs_total` (did anything call it) and `evictions_total{reason}` (did it do anything). Neither substitutes: a broken pass completes normally and returns 0. Since nothing calls `run_eviction_pass` today, that counter would be **absent rather than zero** — phase 4 must alert on absence, which a naive `rate()` threshold silently misses.
- **`mr-cache-revalidation-checks` costs new code, and I recommended it anyway.** It's the only *direct* detector of the critical failure. Every other staleness signal infers divergence from a cause I anticipated; this one observes divergence itself, so it catches mechanisms this analysis missed. The proxies go green the moment the evictor is fixed even if divergence persists for another reason.

Phase 4 -- alert recommendations: for every non-excluded failure mode, recommend at
least one alert rule detecting it, naming the failure mode(s) it serves; an alert

may go silently unmapped. Propose every entry through `propose_edits`, tagged for

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.

  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.

Write every alert expression as PromQL — this stack's expression language.

Each recommended alert is an `AlertRuleInput` with every one of these fields
populated:

- `name`: the alert's identifier.
- `expr`: the PromQL expression that fires the alert, at most
  5000 characters. Split an alert that would need more into
  several smaller ones rather than writing one long expression.
- `for_duration`: how long the expression must hold before firing, as a Prometheus
  duration (e.g. `5m`).

annotations.summary: kvstore is serving values that no longer match storage
annotations.description: The only DIRECT detection of the system's most serious failure -- every other staleness rule infers divergence from a known cause, whereas this observes divergence itself and will therefore catch mechanisms this analysis did not anticipate. payload_or_id.name: KvstoreGetValueErrorRatio
payload_or_id.title: Clients are receiving read errors

annotations.summary: More than 1% of kvstore get_value calls are failing
annotations.description: The ONLY rule in this set deployable today with no code change -- it uses the single implemented metric, kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome}. payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStorageReadErrors
payload_or_id.title: Storage read failures at the boundary

annotations.summary: kvstore storage reads are failing
annotations.description: Measures the failure where it occurs rather than where it happens to reach a client, so unlike KvstoreGetValueErrorRatio this rate is independent of the cache hit ratio and reflects the true severity of the storage problem. payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStorageWriteErrors
payload_or_id.title: Storage writes are failing

annotations.summary: kvstore storage writes are failing; updates are being lost silently
annotations.description: Fires on ANY write error rather than on a ratio, deliberately: writes are low-volume and every failed one is a lost update, and this failure is otherwise completely silent -- StorageError from put() propagates out to the out-of-repo sync job and the read path keeps serving previous values as apparent successes, so every other health signal stays green during a total write outage. payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStorageRecordsDropped
payload_or_id.title: Backing file lost records

annotations.summary: kvstore backing file record count dropped
annotations.description: Records only disappear through a failure: a truncated or interrupted whole-file rewrite, an ENOSPC mid-write, a lost-update race, or deletion of the file. Warning severity rests on the unverified assumption that the single sync job writes serially; if a second writer is ever added, raise this to critical and add real locking.

annotations.description: The exact signature of the seconds-versus-milliseconds bug in evictor.py: `now` is time.time() in seconds while Entry.inserted_at_ms is milliseconds, so the expiry condition is never true, expired_keys is always empty, and the pass returns 0 while reporting success. The three conjuncts matter together -- passes are running, entries older than TTL_SECONDS exist, and yet zero TTL evictions occurred -- because any one alone has an innocent explanation. The absent() branch covers the current state where the counter has never been incremented and so has no series. The `on()` matching assumes a single instance; add instance to the matchers if this runs replicated.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreCacheEntriesExceedTTL
payload_or_id.title: Cached entries far older than the configured TTL

annotations.summary: kvstore oldest cache entry is more than twice the TTL
annotations.description: If expiry worked, this value could never exceed TTL_SECONDS (300). Exceeding it is direct proof that entries are not being expired, and it holds whichever evictor failure is responsible -- broken arithmetic or no scheduler -- which is why it is the single most valuable rule in this set. It is also the staleness bound: an entry's age is the maximum time it can have been diverging from storage, so this is the closest thing to an SLO on how stale a served value can be. Threshold is 2x TTL to tolerate pass interval jitter; tighten it toward TTL once the eviction interval is known. IMPORTANT: the gauge backing this alert reads the same timestamp field the buggy comparison uses, so it is vulnerable to the identical unit error -- unit-test it against an entry older than the TTL before trusting a green result.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreWritesWithoutCacheInvalidation
payload_or_id.title: Writes are landing with no matching cache invalidation

annotations.summary: kvstore writes succeeded but no cache entries were invalidated
annotations.description: A reconciliation between two counters rather than a threshold on one: admin.update_value writes to storage and never calls cache.evict(key), despite receiving the Cache as an argument, so every write to a cached key creates an immediate and permanent divergence. In the current code the reason="write" series cannot exist at all, which is why the absent() branch is required. This is the root link of the staleness chain and fires long before any client notices a wrong value -- treat it as the earliest actionable point in that chain.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStaleCacheEntriesDetected
payload_or_id.title: Revalidation found cached values diverging from storage

annotations.summary: kvstore is serving values that no longer match storage
annotations.description: The only DIRECT detection of the system's most serious failure -- every other staleness rule infers divergence from a known cause, whereas this observes divergence itself and will therefore catch mechanisms this analysis did not anticipate. Fires on any non-zero count with the shortest usable for-duration, deliberately: this is a sampled check, so one observed stale entry implies a population of them, and with no working expiry the divergence is permanent rather than transient. Do not add a ratio threshold -- the sample size is small by design and a percentage would mask real divergence.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreVanishedCacheEntriesDetected
payload_or_id.title: Revalidation found cached keys missing from storage

annotations.summary: kvstore holds cached entries for keys no longer present in storage
annotations.description: Separated from the stale-value alert because the causes and the response differ: this fires when a key the cache believes in has disappeared from the backing file, which points at record loss (truncated rewrite, ENOSPC, lost update) rather than at a missed invalidation. It also covers the inverse client symptom -- a cached None that persists after the sync job creates the key -- which is otherwise indistinguishable from a legitimately absent key, since get_value returns None and counts outcome="success" in both cases. Cross-check kvstore_storage_records for a drop before treating it as a cache-only problem.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreNegativeCacheInflation
payload_or_id.title: Cache dominated by entries for keys that do not exist

annotations.summary: kvstore cache holds far more entries than storage has records, or most reads are not-found
annotations.description: Cache.get caches the miss itself as Entry(value=None), so keys that do not exist occupy cache slots permanently. Two signatures, either sufficient: entry count far exceeding the record count (cache penetration inflating memory), or a not-found rate above half of all traffic (scanning or probing for absent keys). Scoped to this warning-severity failure mode only, so it does not page -- the critical consequence, a real key reading as absent, is covered by KvstoreVanishedCacheEntriesDetected. Both thresholds need tuning against the real key space; the 10x ratio assumes the working set is a modest fraction of stored records.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreGetValueErrorRatio
payload_or_id.title: Clients are receiving read errors

annotations.summary: More than 1% of kvstore get_value calls are failing
annotations.description: The ONLY rule in this set deployable today with no code change -- it uses the single implemented metric, kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome}. StorageError from the backing file is propagating to clients. Critical severity caveat for the runbook: the cache masks the blast radius, because already-cached keys keep being served from memory during a storage outage, so this ratio scales with the miss rate and systematically UNDERSTATES severity -- a completely broken backing file can present here as a few percent. Check KvstoreStorageReadErrors, which measures the failure at its source, before judging the scale.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStorageReadErrors
payload_or_id.title: Storage read failures at the boundary

annotations.summary: kvstore storage reads are failing
annotations.description: Measures the failure where it occurs rather than where it happens to reach a client, so unlike KvstoreGetValueErrorRatio this rate is independent of the cache hit ratio and reflects the true severity of the storage problem. Causes: permissions change, EIO, unmounted or read-only filesystem, the path replaced by a directory. Note one variant this alert CANNOT see -- Storage.get treats a missing file as an empty store and returns None without raising, so outright deletion of the dataset produces no errors here at all; KvstoreStorageRecordsDropped covers that case.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStorageWriteErrors
payload_or_id.title: Storage writes are failing

annotations.summary: kvstore storage writes are failing; updates are being lost silently
annotations.description: Fires on ANY write error rather than on a ratio, deliberately: writes are low-volume and every failed one is a lost update, and this failure is otherwise completely silent -- StorageError from put() propagates out to the out-of-repo sync job and the read path keeps serving previous values as apparent successes, so every other health signal stays green during a total write outage. Check disk space first (ENOSPC is a likely cause and is especially dangerous here, because put() rewrites the whole file and can truncate the existing dataset rather than merely rejecting the new record), then permissions and mount state.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStorageRecordsDropped
payload_or_id.title: Backing file lost records

annotations.summary: kvstore backing file record count dropped
annotations.description: Records only disappear through a failure: a truncated or interrupted whole-file rewrite, an ENOSPC mid-write, a lost-update race, or deletion of the file. The second clause catches the dataset going to zero, which is the case that produces NO errors anywhere -- Storage.get treats a missing file as an empty store and returns None with outcome="success", so without this rule total data loss presents as a perfectly healthy service answering every read with None. Silent on the read path for any key still cached, so the record count is the only timely signal. Restore from backup before the cache turns over and the loss becomes client-visible.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreLostUpdateSuspected
payload_or_id.title: Records lost while writes were succeeding

annotations.summary: kvstore lost records during a period of successful, error-free writes
annotations.description: Storage.put is an unsynchronised read-modify-write over the whole file, so two overlapping writers each rewrite from their own snapshot and the later one erases the earlier one's key. The conjunction is the signal: records disappeared, writes reported success, and no write errors occurred -- which rules out the truncation and ENOSPC explanations and leaves the race. Stated limitation, carried from phase 3: this is a WEAK detector and will not catch a lost overwrite of an existing key, since the record count does not change in that case. Warning severity rests on the unverified assumption that the single sync job writes serially; if a second writer is ever added, raise this to critical and add real locking.

payload_or_id.name: KvstorePartialWriteDetected
payload_or_id.title: Unparseable line in the backing file

annotations.summary: kvstore read an unparseable line from the backing file
annotations.description: The fingerprint of an interrupted whole-file rewrite. Storage.put writes directly to the live path with no temp file, no os.replace and no fsync, so the file is observably partial for the duration of every write and any interruption leaves it permanently partial. An unparseable line means the dataset is already damaged and other records may be gone -- check kvstore_storage_records for a drop. The remedy is the write-to-temp-and-rename fix, not tuning this alert: the unsafe write itself emits no signal, so this necessarily detects the damage after the fact rather than the risk.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreKeyDelimiterCollision
payload_or_id.title: A key containing the field delimiter was written

annotations.summary: kvstore wrote a key containing ',' -- reads of a shorter key can return the wrong value
annotations.description: Critical because the consequence is a silent wrong answer that may cross tenant or entity boundaries: storing key "a,b" produces the line "a,b,v", and a later read of key "a" matches that line via partition(',') and returns "b,v" with no error and outcome="success". Detected at WRITE time by necessity -- the resulting line is syntactically perfect, so no read-side metric or parser check can ever identify it, and by the time a client receives the wrong value there is nothing left to observe. Any non-zero count is actionable: identify the offending key and escape or reject it.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreFormatCorruptionWritten
payload_or_id.title: Data breaking the flat-file format was written

annotations.summary: kvstore wrote a value that breaks the key,value-per-line format
annotations.description: The format has no escaping or quoting on either side. A newline inside a value injects an extra line that the next read parses as a genuine record, silently creating a key nobody wrote. Fires at the point of introduction, which is what makes this diagnosable at all: corruption is written now and only surfaces as a wrong answer much later, by which time it is typically attributed to something else entirely. Warning rather than critical because the delimiter-in-key variant, which produces a directly wrong answer, has its own critical alert.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreReadLatencyHigh
payload_or_id.title: Client-visible read latency degraded

annotations.summary: kvstore get_value p99 latency above 500ms
annotations.description: The user-visible end of the latency chain. Every cache miss costs a full read_text plus a linear scan of the whole file, so miss latency grows linearly with the number of stored keys, and a cold cache converts a traffic burst into a burst of whole-file reads. Split by the source label to attribute: rising cache_hit latency points at process pressure, rising storage_read latency at dataset growth, and an unchanged per-source latency with a worse aggregate means the hit ratio collapsed. Threshold is a placeholder -- set it from the client's actual requirement, since no SLO is documented anywhere in this repository.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStorageScanCostRising
payload_or_id.title: Storage operations slowing as the dataset grows

annotations.summary: kvstore storage operation p99 above 200ms
annotations.description: The upstream link behind client-visible latency, alerted separately so it fires first. Both operations are O(dataset size) with the whole file resident in memory: get() reads and scans everything, put() reads everything and rewrites it. Correlate with kvstore_storage_records, which is the underlying driver and the true leading indicator -- if records are growing steadily, this will keep degrading and the fix is a real index or datastore, not a threshold change. Long for-duration because the cache legitimately masks this most of the time and short spikes after a restart are expected.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreColdCacheStampede
payload_or_id.title: Hit ratio collapsed after a restart

annotations.summary: kvstore cache hit ratio below 50% following a restart
annotations.description: The cache is process-local with no warmup and no persistence, so every restart drops it to empty and each subsequent request becomes a full-file read; concurrent misses for the same key are not coalesced, so N simultaneous requests do N independent reads. A brief version of this is EXPECTED after every deploy, which is why the rule is gated on a recent restart and carries a 15m for-duration -- it should fire only when the cache is failing to warm up rather than on every normal restart. If it fires routinely after deploys, lengthen for_duration rather than removing the gate; if it fires with no restart, the cause is not a stampede and KvstoreNegativeCacheInflation is the better lead.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreSyncJobStalled
payload_or_id.title: No successful write in too long

annotations.summary: kvstore has not recorded a successful write in over 2 hours
annotations.description: The out-of-repo data-sync job is the only source of writes, so if it stops, clients read progressively older data with no error anywhere and every other signal stays green. Time-since-last-write is used rather than a rate because the job's cadence is unknown and a rate over a short window would flap for an infrequent job. STATED LIMITATION: this cannot distinguish 'the job ran and had nothing to write' from 'the job did not run' -- only a heartbeat emitted by the job itself closes that gap, and the job is outside this repository. Set the 7200s threshold to several times the real sync interval once known; if the job is genuinely irregular, this alert will be noisy and a heartbeat is the correct fix rather than a longer window.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreInstrumentationRegressed
payload_or_id.title: Correctness instrumentation missing from the deployed build

annotations.summary: kvstore is running without the correctness instrumentation the alert set depends on
annotations.description: Guards the alert set against silent regression. The deployed build increments outcome="success" for every call that does not raise -- including stale values, poisoned None responses, and collision-induced wrong values -- so without the added labels and the revalidation check, the service's only health signal reports 100% success precisely while clients are served wrong data, and the operator concludes the system is healthy. Fires if a rollback or refactor drops any of the three correctness metrics, because their absence looks identical to everything being fine. Long for-duration so ordinary deploy gaps do not trigger it.

event.text:
Phase 4 accepted — **24 alert rules, all 24 non-excluded failure modes mapped, none silently unmapped.** 15 critical, 9 warning.

**Deploy order matters more than the rule count here.**

**Today, no code change:** `KvstoreGetValueErrorRatio` is the only rule in the set that works against current instrumentation.

**First change, unblocks everything else:** `mr-metrics-exposition`. Until the registry is served, 23 of these 24 rules cannot fire — and `KvstoreMetricsAbsent` exists precisely because silence and health are indistinguishable otherwise.

**Highest value per unit of work:** `KvstoreCacheEntriesExceedTTL`. One gauge, one threshold, and it catches both evictor failures at once — if expiry worked, oldest-entry-age could never exceed 300s. It also doubles as the staleness bound, since an entry's age is the maximum time it can have been diverging from storage.

**Three deliberate structural choices:**

- **Absence, not low rate, in three rules.** `KvstoreEvictionPassNotRunning`, `KvstoreWritesWithoutCacheInvalidation`, and `KvstoreEvictionPassEvictsNothing` all carry `absent()` branches. In the current code those series don't exist at all — nothing calls `run_eviction_pass`, and `evictions_total{reason="write"}` can never increment because `update_value` never calls `evict()`. A `rate() == 0` threshold would silently never fire on a series that was never created, which is exactly the failure being hunted.
- **Two evictor alerts, not one.** Liveness and work-done are independently defeasible; a broken pass completes normally and returns 0.
- **`KvstoreInstrumentationRegressed`** guards the set against itself. If a rollback drops the correctness metrics, the service reverts to reporting 100% success while serving wrong data — and every other alert here goes quiet in a way that looks like health.

**Where I bounded severity deliberately:** `KvstoreNegativeCacheInflation` is scoped to the warning-severity failure mode alone so it doesn't page. Its critical consequence — a real key reading as absent — is carried by `KvstoreVanishedCacheEntriesDetected` instead. Widening it would have forced a critical page onto a noisy ratio.

**Carrying forward, unresolved:**

- **Every threshold is a placeholder.** No SLO is documented anywhere in this repo, so `> 0.5` for p99 latency, `1e6` cache entries, and `7200s` since last write are starting points, not recommendations. They need tuning against real steady-state behaviour.
- **`KvstoreSyncJobStalled` cannot distinguish "job ran with nothing to write" from "job didn't run."** Only a heartbeat from the job closes that, and the job is out-of-repo. If its cadence is irregular, this rule will be noisy and the fix is the heartbeat, not a longer window.
- **`KvstoreLostUpdateSuspected` is a weak detector** and won't catch a lost overwrite of an existing key. Its warning severity rests on the assumption the sync job writes serially — the same assumption I flagged at the end of phase 1 and never resolved.
- **`on()` matching assumes a single instance** in four rules; add `instance` to the matchers if this runs replicated.

One thing I'd flag as a caution on the whole set: `KvstoreCacheEntriesExceedTTL` and `KvstoreEvictionPassEvictsNothing` both depend on a gauge that reads the same timestamp field the buggy comparison uses. That gauge is vulnerable to the identical seconds-vs-milliseconds error. If it's written carelessly, you get a green detector for a broken evictor — worse than no alert, because it looks like coverage. Unit-test it against an entry older than the TTL before trusting it.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreTargetDown
payload_or_id.title: Scrape target down -- process dead or exposition broken

annotations.summary: kvstore scrape target is down; get_value is likely unavailable
annotations.description: The process is not answering scrapes. get_value is the only client-facing operation, so if the process is dead every read is failing. This signal cannot by itself distinguish process death from the metrics endpoint alone being broken -- check the process before concluding it is only an observability failure. Deliberately a late detector: it fires when the service is ALREADY down. The preventable path is KvstoreCacheGrowthUnbounded, which fires hours earlier for the memory-exhaustion cause.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreRestartLoop
payload_or_id.title: Process restarting repeatedly (OOM-kill signature)

annotations.summary: kvstore has restarted more than twice in an hour
annotations.description: Repeated restarts with no deploy are the signature of the OOM chain: the cache is unbounded, so resident memory rises until the process is killed, restarts with an empty cache, and repeats. Correlate with process_resident_memory_bytes immediately before each restart and with kvstore_cache_entries. Each restart also empties the cache, so expect a latency spike and a burst of whole-file storage reads after every one. Uses a default collector metric that comes free with prometheus_client -- no instrumentation change needed.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreCacheGrowthUnbounded
payload_or_id.title: Cache entry count growing without bound

annotations.summary: kvstore cache is growing monotonically with no eviction
annotations.description: Nothing bounds this cache: the evictor never expires anything, and misses are cached too, so the entry count tracks every distinct key ever requested for the life of the process. This is the early link in the chain that ends in an OOM kill, and it is the alert that makes that outcome preventable rather than merely detectable -- it should fire hours to days before KvstoreRestartLoop. Both thresholds (1e6 absolute, 1e5 with sustained positive slope) are placeholders: tune them from observed steady-state entry count and the container memory limit, and prefer a threshold derived from bytes-per-entry times the limit once you have measured it.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreEvictionPassNotRunning
payload_or_id.title: Nothing is invoking the eviction pass

annotations.summary: kvstore eviction pass has not run in the last hour
annotations.description: The eviction pass is the only mechanism bounding cache size and entry staleness. The absent() clause is the important half and is not decoration: no module in the repository calls run_eviction_pass at all, so in the current code this counter would be ABSENT rather than zero, and a plain rate-based threshold would silently never fire -- the exact failure this alert exists to catch. Deliberately separate from KvstoreEvictionPassEvictsNothing: this answers 'did anything call the pass', not 'did the pass do any work'. A pass can run perfectly on schedule and still evict nothing.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreEvictionPassEvictsNothing
payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass runs but never evicts (unit-mismatch signature)
payload_or_id.expr: (increase(kvstore_eviction_pass_runs_total{outcome="success"}[6h]) > 0 and on() min_over_time(kvstore_cache_oldest_entry_age_seconds[6h]) > 300 and on() increase(kvstore_cache_evictions_total{reason="ttl"}[6h]) == 0) or (increase(kvstore_eviction_pass_runs_total{outcome="success"}[6h]) > 0 and on() absent(kvstore_cache_evictions_total{reason="ttl"}))

annotations.summary: kvstore eviction passes complete but evict nothing while entries exceed the TTL
annotations.description: The exact signature of the seconds-versus-milliseconds bug in evictor.py: `now` is time.time() in seconds while Entry.inserted_at_ms is milliseconds, so the expiry condition is never true, expired_keys is always empty, and the pass returns 0 while reporting success. The three conjuncts matter together -- passes are running, entries older than TTL_SECONDS exist, and yet zero TTL evictions occurred -- because any one alone has an innocent explanation. The absent() branch covers the current state where the counter has never been incremented and so has no series. The `on()` matching assumes a single instance; add instance to the matchers if this runs replicated.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreCacheEntriesExceedTTL
payload_or_id.title: Cached entries far older than the configured TTL

annotations.summary: kvstore oldest cache entry is more than twice the TTL
annotations.description: If expiry worked, this value could never exceed TTL_SECONDS (300). Exceeding it is direct proof that entries are not being expired, and it holds whichever evictor failure is responsible -- broken arithmetic or no scheduler -- which is why it is the single most valuable rule in this set. It is also the staleness bound: an entry's age is the maximum time it can have been diverging from storage, so this is the closest thing to an SLO on how stale a served value can be. Threshold is 2x TTL to tolerate pass interval jitter; tighten it toward TTL once the eviction interval is known. IMPORTANT: the gauge backing this alert reads the same timestamp field the buggy comparison uses, so it is vulnerable to the identical unit error -- unit-test it against an entry older than the TTL before trusting a green result.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreWritesWithoutCacheInvalidation
payload_or_id.title: Writes are landing with no matching cache invalidation

annotations.summary: kvstore writes succeeded but no cache entries were invalidated
annotations.description: A reconciliation between two counters rather than a threshold on one: admin.update_value writes to storage and never calls cache.evict(key), despite receiving the Cache as an argument, so every write to a cached key creates an immediate and permanent divergence. In the current code the reason="write" series cannot exist at all, which is why the absent() branch is required. This is the root link of the staleness chain and fires long before any client notices a wrong value -- treat it as the earliest actionable point in that chain.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStaleCacheEntriesDetected
payload_or_id.title: Revalidation found cached values diverging from storage

annotations.summary: kvstore is serving values that no longer match storage
annotations.description: The only DIRECT detection of the system's most serious failure -- every other staleness rule infers divergence from a known cause, whereas this observes divergence itself and will therefore catch mechanisms this analysis did not anticipate. Fires on any non-zero count with the shortest usable for-duration, deliberately: this is a sampled check, so one observed stale entry implies a population of them, and with no working expiry the divergence is permanent rather than transient. Do not add a ratio threshold -- the sample size is small by design and a percentage would mask real divergence.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreVanishedCacheEntriesDetected
payload_or_id.title: Revalidation found cached keys missing from storage

annotations.summary: kvstore holds cached entries for keys no longer present in storage
annotations.description: Separated from the stale-value alert because the causes and the response differ: this fires when a key the cache believes in has disappeared from the backing file, which points at record loss (truncated rewrite, ENOSPC, lost update) rather than at a missed invalidation. It also covers the inverse client symptom -- a cached None that persists after the sync job creates the key -- which is otherwise indistinguishable from a legitimately absent key, since get_value returns None and counts outcome="success" in both cases. Cross-check kvstore_storage_records for a drop before treating it as a cache-only problem.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreNegativeCacheInflation
payload_or_id.title: Cache dominated by entries for keys that do not exist

annotations.summary: kvstore cache holds far more entries than storage has records, or most reads are not-found
annotations.description: Cache.get caches the miss itself as Entry(value=None), so keys that do not exist occupy cache slots permanently. Two signatures, either sufficient: entry count far exceeding the record count (cache penetration inflating memory), or a not-found rate above half of all traffic (scanning or probing for absent keys). Scoped to this warning-severity failure mode only, so it does not page -- the critical consequence, a real key reading as absent, is covered by KvstoreVanishedCacheEntriesDetected. Both thresholds need tuning against the real key space; the 10x ratio assumes the working set is a modest fraction of stored records.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreGetValueErrorRatio
payload_or_id.title: Clients are receiving read errors

annotations.summary: More than 1% of kvstore get_value calls are failing
annotations.description: The ONLY rule in this set deployable today with no code change -- it uses the single implemented metric, kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome}. StorageError from the backing file is propagating to clients. Critical severity caveat for the runbook: the cache masks the blast radius, because already-cached keys keep being served from memory during a storage outage, so this ratio scales with the miss rate and systematically UNDERSTATES severity -- a completely broken backing file can present here as a few percent. Check KvstoreStorageReadErrors, which measures the failure at its source, before judging the scale.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStorageReadErrors
payload_or_id.title: Storage read failures at the boundary

annotations.summary: kvstore storage reads are failing
annotations.description: Measures the failure where it occurs rather than where it happens to reach a client, so unlike KvstoreGetValueErrorRatio this rate is independent of the cache hit ratio and reflects the true severity of the storage problem. Causes: permissions change, EIO, unmounted or read-only filesystem, the path replaced by a directory. Note one variant this alert CANNOT see -- Storage.get treats a missing file as an empty store and returns None without raising, so outright deletion of the dataset produces no errors here at all; KvstoreStorageRecordsDropped covers that case.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStorageWriteErrors
payload_or_id.title: Storage writes are failing

annotations.summary: kvstore storage writes are failing; updates are being lost silently
annotations.description: Fires on ANY write error rather than on a ratio, deliberately: writes are low-volume and every failed one is a lost update, and this failure is otherwise completely silent -- StorageError from put() propagates out to the out-of-repo sync job and the read path keeps serving previous values as apparent successes, so every other health signal stays green during a total write outage. Check disk space first (ENOSPC is a likely cause and is especially dangerous here, because put() rewrites the whole file and can truncate the existing dataset rather than merely rejecting the new record), then permissions and mount state.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStorageRecordsDropped
payload_or_id.title: Backing file lost records

annotations.summary: kvstore backing file record count dropped
annotations.description: Records only disappear through a failure: a truncated or interrupted whole-file rewrite, an ENOSPC mid-write, a lost-update race, or deletion of the file. The second clause catches the dataset going to zero, which is the case that produces NO errors anywhere -- Storage.get treats a missing file as an empty store and returns None with outcome="success", so without this rule total data loss presents as a perfectly healthy service answering every read with None. Silent on the read path for any key still cached, so the record count is the only timely signal. Restore from backup before the cache turns over and the loss becomes client-visible.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreLostUpdateSuspected
payload_or_id.title: Records lost while writes were succeeding

annotations.summary: kvstore lost records during a period of successful, error-free writes
annotations.description: Storage.put is an unsynchronised read-modify-write over the whole file, so two overlapping writers each rewrite from their own snapshot and the later one erases the earlier one's key. The conjunction is the signal: records disappeared, writes reported success, and no write errors occurred -- which rules out the truncation and ENOSPC explanations and leaves the race. Stated limitation, carried from phase 3: this is a WEAK detector and will not catch a lost overwrite of an existing key, since the record count does not change in that case. Warning severity rests on the unverified assumption that the single sync job writes serially; if a second writer is ever added, raise this to critical and add real locking.

payload_or_id.name: KvstorePartialWriteDetected
payload_or_id.title: Unparseable line in the backing file

annotations.summary: kvstore read an unparseable line from the backing file
annotations.description: The fingerprint of an interrupted whole-file rewrite. Storage.put writes directly to the live path with no temp file, no os.replace and no fsync, so the file is observably partial for the duration of every write and any interruption leaves it permanently partial. An unparseable line means the dataset is already damaged and other records may be gone -- check kvstore_storage_records for a drop. The remedy is the write-to-temp-and-rename fix, not tuning this alert: the unsafe write itself emits no signal, so this necessarily detects the damage after the fact rather than the risk.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreKeyDelimiterCollision
payload_or_id.title: A key containing the field delimiter was written

annotations.summary: kvstore wrote a key containing ',' -- reads of a shorter key can return the wrong value
annotations.description: Critical because the consequence is a silent wrong answer that may cross tenant or entity boundaries: storing key "a,b" produces the line "a,b,v", and a later read of key "a" matches that line via partition(',') and returns "b,v" with no error and outcome="success". Detected at WRITE time by necessity -- the resulting line is syntactically perfect, so no read-side metric or parser check can ever identify it, and by the time a client receives the wrong value there is nothing left to observe. Any non-zero count is actionable: identify the offending key and escape or reject it.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreFormatCorruptionWritten
payload_or_id.title: Data breaking the flat-file format was written

annotations.summary: kvstore wrote a value that breaks the key,value-per-line format
annotations.description: The format has no escaping or quoting on either side. A newline inside a value injects an extra line that the next read parses as a genuine record, silently creating a key nobody wrote. Fires at the point of introduction, which is what makes this diagnosable at all: corruption is written now and only surfaces as a wrong answer much later, by which time it is typically attributed to something else entirely. Warning rather than critical because the delimiter-in-key variant, which produces a directly wrong answer, has its own critical alert.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreReadLatencyHigh
payload_or_id.title: Client-visible read latency degraded

annotations.summary: kvstore get_value p99 latency above 500ms
annotations.description: The user-visible end of the latency chain. Every cache miss costs a full read_text plus a linear scan of the whole file, so miss latency grows linearly with the number of stored keys, and a cold cache converts a traffic burst into a burst of whole-file reads. Split by the source label to attribute: rising cache_hit latency points at process pressure, rising storage_read latency at dataset growth, and an unchanged per-source latency with a worse aggregate means the hit ratio collapsed. Threshold is a placeholder -- set it from the client's actual requirement, since no SLO is documented anywhere in this repository.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStorageScanCostRising
payload_or_id.title: Storage operations slowing as the dataset grows

annotations.summary: kvstore storage operation p99 above 200ms
annotations.description: The upstream link behind client-visible latency, alerted separately so it fires first. Both operations are O(dataset size) with the whole file resident in memory: get() reads and scans everything, put() reads everything and rewrites it. Correlate with kvstore_storage_records, which is the underlying driver and the true leading indicator -- if records are growing steadily, this will keep degrading and the fix is a real index or datastore, not a threshold change. Long for-duration because the cache legitimately masks this most of the time and short spikes after a restart are expected.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreColdCacheStampede
payload_or_id.title: Hit ratio collapsed after a restart

annotations.summary: kvstore cache hit ratio below 50% following a restart
annotations.description: The cache is process-local with no warmup and no persistence, so every restart drops it to empty and each subsequent request becomes a full-file read; concurrent misses for the same key are not coalesced, so N simultaneous requests do N independent reads. A brief version of this is EXPECTED after every deploy, which is why the rule is gated on a recent restart and carries a 15m for-duration -- it should fire only when the cache is failing to warm up rather than on every normal restart. If it fires routinely after deploys, lengthen for_duration rather than removing the gate; if it fires with no restart, the cause is not a stampede and KvstoreNegativeCacheInflation is the better lead.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreSyncJobStalled
payload_or_id.title: No successful write in too long

annotations.summary: kvstore has not recorded a successful write in over 2 hours
annotations.description: The out-of-repo data-sync job is the only source of writes, so if it stops, clients read progressively older data with no error anywhere and every other signal stays green. Time-since-last-write is used rather than a rate because the job's cadence is unknown and a rate over a short window would flap for an infrequent job. STATED LIMITATION: this cannot distinguish 'the job ran and had nothing to write' from 'the job did not run' -- only a heartbeat emitted by the job itself closes that gap, and the job is outside this repository. Set the 7200s threshold to several times the real sync interval once known; if the job is genuinely irregular, this alert will be noisy and a heartbeat is the correct fix rather than a longer window.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreInstrumentationRegressed
payload_or_id.title: Correctness instrumentation missing from the deployed build

annotations.summary: kvstore is running without the correctness instrumentation the alert set depends on
annotations.description: Guards the alert set against silent regression. Fires if a rollback or refactor drops any of the three correctness metrics, because their absence looks identical to everything being fine. Long for-duration so ordinary deploy gaps do not trigger it.

annotations.summary: kvstore read an unparseable line from the backing file
annotations.description: The fingerprint of an interrupted whole-file rewrite. Storage.put writes directly to the live path with no temp file, no os.replace and no fsync, so the file is observably partial for the duration of every write and any interruption leaves it permanently partial. An unparseable line means the dataset is already damaged and other records may be gone -- check kvstore_storage_records for a drop. The remedy is the write-to-temp-and-rename fix, not tuning this alert: the unsafe write itself emits no signal, so this necessarily detects the damage after the fact rather than the risk.

annotations.description: Critical because the consequence is a silent wrong answer that may cross tenant or entity boundaries: storing key "a,b" produces the line "a,b,v", and a later read of key "a" matches that line via partition(',') and returns "b,v" with no error and outcome="success". Detected at WRITE time by necessity -- the resulting line is syntactically perfect, so no read-side metric or parser check can ever identify it, and by the time a client receives the wrong value there is nothing left to observe. Any non-zero count is actionable: identify the offending key and escape or reject it.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreFormatCorruptionWritten

annotations.summary: kvstore wrote a value that breaks the key,value-per-line format
annotations.description: The format has no escaping or quoting on either side. A newline inside a value injects an extra line that the next read parses as a genuine record, silently creating a key nobody wrote. Fires at the point of introduction, which is what makes this diagnosable at all: corruption is written now and only surfaces as a wrong answer much later, by which time it is typically attributed to something else entirely. Warning rather than critical because the delimiter-in-key variant, which produces a directly wrong answer, has its own critical alert.

annotations.summary: kvstore get_value p99 latency above 500ms
annotations.description: The user-visible end of the latency chain. Every cache miss costs a full read_text plus a linear scan of the whole file, so miss latency grows linearly with the number of stored keys, and a cold cache converts a traffic burst into a burst of whole-file reads. Split by the source label to attribute: rising cache_hit latency points at process pressure, rising storage_read latency at dataset growth, and an unchanged per-source latency with a worse aggregate means the hit ratio collapsed. Threshold is a placeholder -- set it from the client's actual requirement, since no SLO is documented anywhere in this repository.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreStorageScanCostRising
payload_or_id.title: Storage operations slowing as the dataset grows

annotations.summary: kvstore storage operation p99 above 200ms
annotations.description: The upstream link behind client-visible latency, alerted separately so it fires first. Both operations are O(dataset size) with the whole file resident in memory: get() reads and scans everything, put() reads everything and rewrites it. Correlate with kvstore_storage_records, which is the underlying driver and the true leading indicator -- if records are growing steadily, this will keep degrading and the fix is a real index or datastore, not a threshold change. annotations.summary: kvstore cache hit ratio below 50% following a restart
annotations.description: The cache is process-local with no warmup and no persistence, so every restart drops it to empty and each subsequent request becomes a full-file read; concurrent misses for the same key are not coalesced, so N simultaneous requests do N independent reads. A brief version of this is EXPECTED after every deploy, which is why the rule is gated on a recent restart and carries a 15m for-duration -- it should fire only when the cache is failing to warm up rather than on every normal restart. If it fires routinely after deploys, lengthen for_duration rather than removing the gate; if it fires with no restart, the cause is not a stampede and KvstoreNegativeCacheInflation is the better lead.

Time-since-last-write is used rather than a rate because the job's cadence is unknown and a rate over a short window would flap for an infrequent job.
