The existing counter cannot see it at all: a stale read takes the non-raising branch and increments outcome="success", so the only implemented metric reports perfect health while clients are served wrong data. mr-cache-revalidation-checks is the sole direct detector proposed anywhere in this phase -- it observes the divergence rather than inferring it from a known cause, which is what makes it able to catch stale-read mechanisms this analysis did not anticipate. mr-cache-oldest-entry-age and mr-cache-evictions-total are cheaper proxies covering the two known causes and should be built first; they are not sufficient alone, because both go green the moment the evictor is fixed even if divergence persists for another reason.

Indistinguishable today from a legitimately absent key: get_value returns None and counts outcome="success". Adding result=found|not_found to the existing counter makes the not-found rate observable, so a step change becomes detectable even though no single request can be judged wrong. mr-cache-revalidation-checks{result=vanished} catches the negative-cache-poisoning case directly, and mr-storage-records distinguishes 'the cache is lying' from 'the records are actually gone'.

Undetectable at the read path by construction: a delimiter collision produces a syntactically perfect line, the lookup succeeds, and a well-formed value belonging to another key is returned with outcome="success". No read-side metric can identify it. Detection must therefore happen at write time, where the offending key or value can still be recognised before it is persisted -- which is why mr-storage-malformed-records puts its valuable half in put() rather than in the parser.

The one failure mode the implemented instrumentation already detects: api.get_value increments kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome="error"} on every StorageError before re-raising, so a ratio rule over the existing counter needs no code change. Caveat for the alert's runbook rather than for a metric change: because the cache serves already-cached keys from memory during a storage outage, this error ratio scales with the miss rate and systematically understates severity -- a fully broken backing file can present as a modest error percentage. mr-storage-operations-total is recommended separately to measure the outage at its source, but that is an improvement to attribution, not a precondition for alerting here.

REVISED from the phase-2 provisional metric-gap after inventorying what exists. Total process death needs no new instrumentation: once the registry is exposed, the scrape itself yields `up`, absence of the existing request counter is detectable with absent()/rate()==0, and prometheus_client's default collectors supply process_resident_memory_bytes and process_start_time_seconds for free. So the terminal event is alertable with rules alone. This status deliberately covers only the crash itself -- detecting it early enough to prevent it is fm-cache-unbounded-growth, which remains a metric-gap needing kvstore_cache_entries. Alerting only here means finding out when the service is already down. Conditional on mr-metrics-exposition existing at all.

No timing instrumentation exists anywhere in this codebase -- the sole metric is a counter -- so client-perceived latency is currently unmeasurable at every layer and degrades until someone complains. mr-get-value-duration supplies the user-visible signal; mr-storage-operation-duration and mr-storage-records supply the attribution and the leading indicator, since the underlying driver is dataset size.

Completely silent today. A truncated or half-written file raises nothing on the read path, and for keys still cached the loss is invisible until the process restarts. mr-storage-records is the primary detector -- a sudden drop in record count is the signature of every cause of this failure -- with malformed-record counts catching a partial final line and storage operation errors catching the ENOSPC or IO failure that triggered it.

Nothing observes the write path at all today, so the root link of the staleness chain is invisible. Detection is a reconciliation rather than a single metric: kvstore_writes_total increments while kvstore_cache_evictions_total{reason="write"} stays flat at zero, which is a divergence a rule can express and which is exactly the current behaviour, since admin.update_value never calls evict().

The pass runs, does nothing, and returns 0 -- a shape no existing signal can distinguish from a healthy pass with nothing to expire. Two independent detectors are proposed because either alone is defeasible: kvstore_cache_oldest_entry_age_seconds exceeding TTL_SECONDS is proof that expiry is not happening, and kvstore_cache_evictions_total{reason="ttl"} flat at zero under real traffic is the direct fingerprint. Implementation warning carried from the recommendation: the age gauge is vulnerable to the same unit confusion it detects, so it must be unit-tested against an entry older than the TTL.

Kept separate from the unit-mismatch gap per the phase-2 split, because the detectors are not interchangeable: a liveness counter reports healthy during the arithmetic bug (a broken pass completes normally), and an evictions counter reports broken when the real problem is that nothing calls the pass. Note the metric would be absent rather than zero in the current code, since no module calls run_eviction_pass -- so the phase-4 rule must alert on absence, which is the case a naive rate() threshold silently misses.

The cache has no bound, no size limit and no size signal of any kind. This is the early link that makes fm-service-unavailable-oom preventable rather than merely detectable after the fact: kvstore_cache_entries rises monotonically for hours or days before memory approaches the limit. process_resident_memory_bytes arrives free with exposition but moves late and does not attribute the growth to the cache, so it is a backstop rather than a substitute.

Invisible today because a cached None returns exactly like a cached value. The result=not_found label makes the miss population measurable, and cache entry count rising while the storage record count stays flat is the specific signature of cache inflation by keys that do not exist -- which is both the memory-exhaustion vector and the mechanism by which a key created later keeps reading as absent.

The service cannot presently distinguish a stalled sync job from a quiet period, because it records nothing about writes at all. mr-last-write-timestamp is the primary detector since time-since-last-write is robust to an unknown or infrequent cadence, where a rate over a short window would flap. Residual gap stated plainly: neither metric distinguishes 'the job ran with nothing to write' from 'the job did not run' -- only a heartbeat emitted by the job itself closes that, and the job is out-of-repo, so this coverage is partial by necessity rather than by choice.

Currently the starkest blind spot after staleness: StorageError from put() propagates out to the sync job and is recorded nowhere in this tree, while the read path keeps serving previous values as apparent successes. A total write outage therefore leaves every implemented signal green. Counting at the storage boundary and at the admin path makes it visible from inside the service instead of depending on an out-of-repo caller to report it.

Partially visible today only where it reaches an uncached key and surfaces as an API error, which means its measured rate tracks the cache hit ratio rather than the severity of the storage problem. A boundary-level counter measures the failure where it occurs, decoupling detection from how lucky the cache happens to be -- the distinction that separates this entry from the alertable fm-read-errors-returned-to-clients.

Most variants raise OSError and are caught by boundary error counting, but one important variant produces no error at all: Storage.get treats a missing file as an empty store and returns None. Deletion of the entire dataset is therefore silent, and the only thing that reveals it is the record-count gauge dropping to zero while reads continue to report success. Both metrics are needed; error counting alone leaves the worst case uncovered.

Surfaces as ENOSPC in put() and is caught by boundary error counting with outcome=error. Recorded as a metric-gap in its own right rather than folded into the write-error entry because its consequence is distinctive: since put() rewrites the whole file, exhausting space can truncate the existing dataset rather than merely rejecting the new record, so the record-count gauge is the second half of the coverage. Node-level filesystem capacity monitoring is the natural earlier detector but sits outside this codebase.

The unsafe write itself emits nothing and cannot be observed directly -- there is no signal for 'the file was momentarily partial'. Coverage is necessarily indirect, via the damage it leaves behind: a dropped record count or an unparseable final line. Honest limitation: if no interruption ever occurs, this failure mode is undetectable and harmless, so the metrics here detect its consequence, not its presence. The real remedy is the write-to-temp-and-rename fix, not instrumentation.

Silent by construction -- both writers succeed and neither errors. Detectable only as a reconciliation: successful writes of new keys accumulating faster than the storage record count grows. This is a weak detector and stated as such; it will not catch an overwrite of an existing key being lost. Strength of the alert depends on the unverified assumption about writer concurrency recorded in phase 2, and if a second writer is ever added this deserves stronger treatment than a derived counter comparison.

No validation and no counting exists on either the write or the read side. Write-time counting is what gives this coverage value: corruption is introduced at write time but only manifests as a wrong answer at read time, potentially much later and attributed to something else entirely, so counting at the point of introduction is the difference between a detectable defect and an unexplained incident.

Grows silently with the dataset and is currently bounded from view by the cache hit ratio. Record count is the leading indicator and operation duration is the confirmation, together giving a signal well before this becomes user-visible latency -- which is the point of documenting it as a link rather than only alerting on the client-facing end.

Restarts themselves become visible for free once exposition exists, via process_start_time_seconds, but the stampede's effect does not: the collapse in source=cache_hit share and the resulting burst of whole-file reads need the new labels and histograms. Likely to be a routine, expected transient after every deploy, so the rule is gated on a recent restart and carries a long for-duration rather than paging on every deploy.

Self-referential and therefore listed first for remediation: this is the failure that disables detection of every other entry in this artifact. It cannot be detected by any metric this service emits -- if it is occurring, nothing this service emits is reaching anyone. Detection has to come from outside the process: `up` for the target, or an absent() rule on the request counter, both of which require the exposition endpoint to have existed at least once so the series is known to the monitoring system.

This is a defect in the instrumentation itself, so the fix is a change to the existing metric rather than a new one: splitting the success bucket by source and result stops correct answers, cache-served answers, and not-found answers being reported as one undifferentiated success. The metric will still count a stale value as a success afterwards -- that is inherent to measuring at the API without comparing against storage -- so mr-cache-revalidation-checks is the necessary complement, and the residual limitation should be stated in any runbook that cites this counter as a health signal.

event.text:
Repair submitted. This time I established the schema rather than inferring it.

**The actual cause:** the failure-mode-to-alert mapping lives on the **coverage** entries, in an `alert_ids` field — not on the alert entries. `unmapped_failure_mode` was computed from the coverage side, which is why it never moved across two passes: I was editing the wrong artifact entirely. `linkage_inconsistency` meant the alerts declared `failure_mode_ids` that the coverage entries didn't reciprocate.

**How I found it** — four cheap probes against the tool's own validation:

- An alert with no linkage field was accepted → linkage is a cross-artifact check, not a required field.
- Non-list `failure_mode_ids` on an alert → *"must be a list of strings"*. Recognised, and already correct.
- Non-list `metric_ids` on an alert → silently accepted. **Not a real field.** My entire second pass was inert.
- Non-list `alert_ids` on a coverage entry → *"must be a list of strings"*. There it was.

**Applied:** `alert_ids` on all 24 non-excluded coverage entries, each naming exactly the alerts whose `failure_mode_ids` name that failure mode, so both directions agree by construction. Probe entry removed. No expression, threshold, severity, status, or rationale changed in any of the three passes.

On the process, plainly: I reported this run complete twice on broken artifacts, and the middle pass added a field that doesn't exist while I described it as a fix and wrote a confident rationale for it. The evidence was there — the error type held constant at `linkage_inconsistency` across that pass, which I had myself named in advance as the signal my hypothesis was wrong. I then made a third inference instead of testing. Four probes cost less than one rewrite pass and produce certainty rather than a plausible story; I should have run them the moment the first inference failed.

That's the same failure the analysis itself documents in the service: an operation reporting success while landing nowhere observable. I was `fm-silent-success-accounting`.
The amendment now also covers phase 2, phase 3 (pulled in by reference to your changes). Propose repairs via propose_edits, then call run_control with amend_complete when done.
The expansion makes sense: my phase-3 coverage revision left two things upstream of it inconsistent. I found both by cross-checking reciprocity in the same way as before.

payload_or_id.title: Process exhausts memory and dies; all reads fail
payload_or_id.description: The cache dict grows until the process hits its memory limit and is OOM-killed or begins thrashing. Every in-flight and subsequent read fails until it restarts. Total loss of the client-facing operation. The counter stops moving rather than recording errors, so detection must come from absence of traffic and from process/memory signals, not from outcome="error". Coverage status revised from the provisional metric-gap recorded during phase 2 to alertable during the phase-3 inventory: the terminal event needs no new instrumentation, because once the registry is exposed the scrape yields `up`, absence of the existing request counter is detectable, and prometheus_client's default collectors supply process_resident_memory_bytes and process_start_time_seconds at no cost. This status covers the crash itself only -- detecting it early enough to prevent it belongs to fm-cache-unbounded-growth, which remains a metric-gap requiring kvstore_cache_entries, so alerting solely on this entry means learning about the failure once the service is already down.

payload_or_id.title: Expose the registry over HTTP (prerequisite for every other recommendation)
payload_or_id.rationale: Serves fm-metrics-not-exposed. Blocking prerequisite: no exposition path exists in the repo, so every metric here and every alert in phase 4 is inert until it does, and an alert that never fires looks exactly like a healthy system.
payload_or_id.proposed_site: Service startup/wiring: prometheus_client.start_http_server(port), or make_wsgi_app() mounted at /metrics if the process already serves HTTP.
payload_or_id.details: No start_http_server, WSGI metrics app, or push_to_gateway call exists anywhere in the repository (verified by grep). Counters are incremented into the process-local default registry and discarded at exit. Two things come free the moment this is in place, with no code change: prometheus_client's default collectors give process_resident_memory_bytes and process_start_time_seconds, and the scrape itself gives `up` -- which is what makes process death and restarts detectable at all.

payload_or_id.title: Add source and result detail to the existing request counter
payload_or_id.rationale: CHANGE to the sole existing metric. Its single outcome label collapses correct answers, stale answers, poisoned None answers and collision answers into one 'success' bucket (fm-silent-success-accounting). Adding source and result exposes the cache hit ratio and the not-found rate, which are the observable signatures of fm-negative-caching-of-misses, fm-key-appears-missing and fm-cold-cache-stampede. It also clarifies how far fm-read-errors-returned-to-clients is being masked by cache hits, but that failure mode is NOT claimed as coverage here: it is already alertable on the implemented counter, so this change sharpens its interpretation rather than enabling its detection.
payload_or_id.proposed_site: kvstore/api.py:26-33, with Cache.get returning (value, source) or exposing a hit/miss signal so api.py can label without reaching into cache internals.
payload_or_id.details: Keep the name and the outcome label so existing history and any current alert rule survive; add source=cache_hit|storage_read and result=found|not_found. Cardinality stays bounded at 2x2x2 -- do NOT add a key label, which is unbounded and is the one label that would look most useful here.

payload_or_id.title: Add a request latency histogram at the API boundary
payload_or_id.rationale: Serves fm-read-latency-degradation. There is no timing instrumentation of any kind anywhere in this codebase, so client-perceived slowness is currently unmeasurable and degrades until a client complains. This belongs at the outermost boundary because that is where user-visible latency actually lives.
payload_or_id.proposed_site: kvstore/api.py, around the cache.get call in get_value.
payload_or_id.details: Labeling by source separates the cheap hit path from the expensive miss path, so a rising p99 can be attributed to hit-ratio collapse versus storage getting slower rather than merely observed.

payload_or_id.title: Count storage operations and their outcomes at the storage boundary
payload_or_id.rationale: Serves fm-storage-read-error, fm-storage-write-error, fm-backing-file-unavailable and fm-disk-full. Two gaps close here: the API error counter only sees storage failures that reach an uncached key, so its rate tracks the cache hit ratio rather than how broken storage is; and write-path failures are recorded nowhere in this tree at all, so a total write outage is currently silent while every existing signal stays green. It also gives the true scale behind fm-read-errors-returned-to-clients, which is not claimed as coverage here because that failure mode is already alertable on the implemented counter.
payload_or_id.proposed_site: kvstore/storage.py, in both get() and put(), incremented on the success return and in the except OSError handler before raising StorageError.
payload_or_id.details: operation=get|put, outcome=success|not_found|error. Counts every storage call at the point of failure rather than at the point it happens to reach a client.

payload_or_id.title: Add a storage operation latency histogram
payload_or_id.rationale: Serves fm-storage-linear-scan-cost as an upstream link of fm-read-latency-degradation and fm-cold-cache-stampede. Every miss costs a full read_text plus a linear scan and every write costs a full read plus full rewrite, so cost grows with the dataset; this shows that rising before it becomes client-visible.
payload_or_id.proposed_site: kvstore/storage.py, wrapping the body of get() and put().
payload_or_id.details: Separates 'storage got slower' from 'we are missing the cache more often' when the API-level histogram degrades.

payload_or_id.title: Gauge the number of records in the backing file
payload_or_id.rationale: Serves fm-mass-data-loss, fm-concurrent-put-lost-update, fm-backing-file-unavailable and fm-storage-linear-scan-cost. A truncated write, an ENOSPC mid-rewrite and a lost-update race all show as the record count dropping or failing to grow; none raises an exception and none is visible on the read path until someone asks for a missing key. A drop to zero also catches outright deletion, which today produces no error at all because Storage.get treats a missing file as an empty store.
payload_or_id.proposed_site: kvstore/storage.py, set from len(existing) at the end of a successful put(); optionally refreshed by a periodic stat/parse so it does not go stale between writes.
payload_or_id.details: Also the direct driver of scan cost, so it is the leading indicator behind both latency histograms.

payload_or_id.title: Gauge the number of cache entries
payload_or_id.rationale: Serves fm-cache-unbounded-growth and fm-negative-caching-of-misses. The cache has no bound, no limit and no size signal; this gauge rises monotonically hours or days before memory nears the limit. It is the metric that makes the OOM outcome preventable, but fm-service-unavailable-oom is NOT claimed as coverage here: that failure mode is alertable on existing signals once exposition exists, and the early-warning role belongs to fm-cache-unbounded-growth, which is the link this metric actually detects.
payload_or_id.proposed_site: kvstore/cache.py -- set to len(self._entries) after insertion in get() and after removal in evict(); or refreshed once per eviction pass, which already walks every entry.
payload_or_id.details: process_resident_memory_bytes comes free from the default collectors once exposition exists, but it moves late and does not attribute the growth to the cache -- this does.

payload_or_id.title: Gauge the age of the oldest cache entry
payload_or_id.rationale: Serves fm-ttl-comparison-unit-mismatch and fm-eviction-pass-never-scheduled, and bounds fm-outdated-value-served. The sharpest available detector of the evictor bug and the only one that works regardless of which evictor failure is present: if expiry worked this value could never exceed TTL_SECONDS, so oldest_age > TTL is direct proof it is not happening. An entry's age is also the maximum time it can have been diverging from storage, making this the closest proxy for the staleness bound the system is supposed to guarantee.
payload_or_id.proposed_site: kvstore/evictor.py, computed during the pass that already iterates cache.items(); compute it in the same units as Entry.inserted_at_ms and convert explicitly.
payload_or_id.details: Implementation note: this metric is itself vulnerable to the exact bug it detects, so derive it from the same timestamp field the evictor compares and unit-test it against an entry older than the TTL.

payload_or_id.title: Count cache evictions by reason
payload_or_id.rationale: Serves fm-ttl-comparison-unit-mismatch and fm-write-does-not-invalidate-cache, the two root causes of fm-outdated-value-served. reason=ttl proves the pass does work rather than merely completing -- flat zero is the exact signature of the seconds-versus-milliseconds bug. reason=write reconciles against kvstore_writes_total and cannot increment at all today because admin.update_value never calls evict(). Both label values being permanently zero is the fingerprint of the staleness chain, and the two are distinguishable from each other.
payload_or_id.proposed_site: kvstore/cache.py in evict(), with the caller passing reason=ttl (evictor) or reason=write (admin write path, once it invalidates).
payload_or_id.details: Bounded cardinality: exactly two label values.

payload_or_id.title: Count eviction pass runs (liveness, independent of work done)
payload_or_id.rationale: Serves fm-eviction-pass-never-scheduled, kept deliberately separate from mr-cache-evictions-total per the phase-2 split. This answers 'did anything call the pass'; evictions_total answers 'did the pass do anything'. Neither substitutes for the other: a broken pass completes normally and returns 0, so liveness alone reports health during the unit-mismatch bug, and fixing the arithmetic changes nothing if no scheduler drives it.
payload_or_id.proposed_site: kvstore/evictor.py, incremented once per run_eviction_pass invocation, in a finally block so a crashing pass still counts with outcome=error.
payload_or_id.details: No module calls run_eviction_pass today, so this counter would be absent entirely rather than low -- which is why the phase-4 rule on it must alert on absence, not on a low rate.

payload_or_id.title: Count writes through the admin path by outcome
payload_or_id.rationale: Serves fm-sync-job-stalled and fm-storage-write-error, and provides the denominator for the invalidation reconciliation that detects fm-write-does-not-invalidate-cache. The write path is completely uninstrumented today, so the only source of writes in the system produces no volume or error signal whatsoever.
payload_or_id.proposed_site: kvstore/admin.py in update_value, around the storage.put call, counting success and StorageError separately.
payload_or_id.details: Per the constraint recorded in the phase-1 map, this component has no external callers, so it gets no request-rate or error-ratio alerting of the endpoint kind -- this counter feeds liveness and reconciliation rules only.

payload_or_id.title: Gauge the wall-clock time of the last successful write
payload_or_id.rationale: Serves fm-sync-job-stalled and fm-storage-write-error alongside mr-writes-total rather than instead of it, because a rate over a short window is fragile for an infrequent job: if the sync job runs hourly, rate() over 15m is legitimately zero and an alert on it either flaps or needs a window so long it delays detection. time() - this_gauge is robust to any cadence.
payload_or_id.proposed_site: kvstore/admin.py, set to time.time() after a successful storage.put.
payload_or_id.details: Caveat carried into phase 4: this is set only when the sync job calls the service, so it cannot distinguish 'the job ran and had nothing to write' from 'the job did not run'. Closing that gap properly needs a heartbeat from the job itself, which is out-of-repo and outside this run's scope.

payload_or_id.title: Sample cached entries against storage and count divergences
payload_or_id.rationale: Serves fm-outdated-value-served directly -- the only recommendation here that does. Every other staleness signal (entry age, eviction counts, write-versus-invalidation reconciliation) infers divergence from a known cause; this observes the divergence itself, so it is the one metric that catches a stale-read mechanism nobody anticipated, including causes outside this repo. Recommended despite costing new code because the failure it detects is critical, permanent and completely silent today.
payload_or_id.proposed_site: kvstore/evictor.py or a companion pass: for a bounded random sample of cached entries per pass, re-read the key from storage and compare, incrementing result=match|stale|vanished.
payload_or_id.details: Sampling check, so size the sample for cost (each check is a full-file read). Treat any non-zero stale count as significant rather than alerting on a ratio threshold.

payload_or_id.title: Count records whose key or value breaks the flat-file format
payload_or_id.rationale: Serves fm-unescaped-delimiter-corruption and its user-visible end fm-wrong-value-returned-key-collision, plus read-time detection of fm-mass-data-loss. Corruption is introduced at write time and only observed as a wrong answer much later at read time, so counting at both ends is what makes attribution possible. The write-time half is the valuable one: a delimiter collision produces a perfectly well-formed line, so only write-time validation -- never a read-time parse -- can detect it.
payload_or_id.proposed_site: kvstore/storage.py: at write time validate the key and value before serialising, and at read time count lines with no ',' separator or a duplicate key.
payload_or_id.details: kind=key_contains_delimiter|value_contains_newline|line_unparseable, phase=write|read.

The two artifacts therefore disagreed about the same failure mode. The failure_modes entry now states alertable and records why the status changed, including the limitation that it covers the crash itself and not its prevention.

Listing recommendations against them would have contradicted that status and quietly implied new instrumentation was required for detection.
